text:
Throughout this module, you've built evaluations that look at
different parts of an agent's work.

You can check an individual tool call, the trajectory of a run,
requirements that carry across a conversation,
and the state the agent ultimately changed.

Now let's see what happens when you put those checks
together on the same task.

Take a Northwind customer who says early in the conversation,
"Don't refund anything until I confirm the amount."

The agent verifies the customer, looks up order 4521,
and finds that the refundable amount is $49.99. So far, so good.

But then it calls process_refund immediately,
before the customer has confirmed anything,
and tells them your $49.99 refund has been processed.

When you check the database, the refund is there for the correct
amount and the correct order. So, several evaluations pass.

The agent chose the right refund tool,
using the correct order and amount.

Customer verification happened before the refund,
and the expected state change exists in the database.

but the session-level check fails because the agent ignored an
instruction the customer gave earlier in the conversation.

That combination of results tells you something very specific about
the failure. The problem isn't which tool the agent chose.

It isn't the refund amount, the identity check,
or whether the refund actually happened.

The problem is that a constraint established earlier in the session
was no longer being respected when the agent acted.

This also helps explain why an overall score by itself can sometimes
hide the most useful information.

Imagine two Northwind runs both received three passing evaluations out
of four. In the first run, the agent used the wrong order ID.

In the second, the refund was correct,
but the customer wasn't verified first.

The pass rate might be identical, but those are two
very different failures.

one points you towards how information is being passed into a tool,
while the other shows you how the agent is sequencing required steps.

When you evaluate a complex agent, the individual results help you
locate where the task broke down.

That brings us back to the evaluation process you've been using
throughout the course. You still begin by investigating what happened.
For a simple response, that might mean reading the answer.

For the kinds of tasks you've seen in this module, it can mean opening
the trace, looking at the tool calls, reconstructing the trajectory,

checking earlier turns in the session,
or looking at the state in the database.

Then you define what correct behavior should have looked like.
Maybe the right Order ID should have been 4521.

Perhaps verification had to happen before process_refund,
or the customer's instruction had to remain active.

or maybe the task wasn't complete unless a refund
row actually appeared.

Once that expectation is clear, you can evaluate it at the scope where
the relevant evidence exists.

That's the deeper pass through the evaluate stage you've been
working on in this module.

You're no longer asking only, "Was the final response good?"
You can ask, did the agent choose the right action?

Did it use the right information? Did all the required steps happen?
Did they happen in the right order?

Did the agent preserve important context across turns?
And did the task produce the state it was supposed to produce?
Think back to the shelter example you started this module with.

If the agent says, "You're booked with Pepper for Saturday at 2 PM",
you now know that evaluating that response is only the beginning.

You can check whether it used the right volunteer record,
whether it checked eligibility before choosing the dog,

whether the booking happened after those requirements were satisfied,
whether a constraint from an earlier turn was still respected,
and finally, whether the booking actually exists.

That's what it means to find and evaluate failures along the way
to completing a task.

And once your evaluations can tell you where the agent succeeds
and where it breaks down,
you have something more useful than a final score.

You have evidence about what needs attention. In the next module,
you'll take that evidence into the improvement stage.

You'll choose a behavior to improve, make a targeted change,
compare the new version with the old one,

and check whether you fixed the problem without creating another
problem somewhere else.
See you in module 5.
